lessons.title: Common Diseases: Avian Influenza, Newcastle, Enteritis
lessons.body: Ostriches in Africa face three major viral and bacterial diseases that can wipe out your flock if you don't act fast. Avian Influenza (bird flu) is caused by influenza A viruses. It spreads through wild birds, contaminated water, and equipment. Symptoms include sudden death, swollen heads, purple wattles, and respiratory distress. In Africa, outbreaks are common near wetlands where wild waterfowl gather. There is no treatment; cull infected birds and report to authorities immediately. Newcastle disease is a paramyxovirus that attacks the respiratory, nervous, and digestive systems. Look for gasping, twisted necks, paralysis, and greenish diarrhoea. Mortality can reach 90% in unvaccinated flocks. Vaccinate with live or killed vaccinesâfollow the manufacturer's schedule. Enteritis is often bacterial (E. coli, Salmonella) or parasitic. It causes watery droppings, dehydration, and weight loss. Common triggers are dirty water, mouldy feed, and overcrowding. Treat with antibiotics like oxytetracycline (20 mg/kg body weight for 5 days) only under vet advice. Prevent by cleaning drinkers daily, using chlorinated water (2-3 ppm), and rotating pastures. In Africa, heat stress worsens these diseases. Provide shade and cool water. Isolate new birds for 30 days. Quarantine sick ones immediately. Keep records of all deaths and symptoms. Early detection saves moneyâa single outbreak can cost you thousands of dollars.

lessons.title: Vaccination Programs and Medications
lessons.body: Vaccination is your cheapest insurance against deadly ostrich diseases. In Africa, core vaccines are Newcastle, Avian Influenza (where permitted), and Fowl Pox. Start chicks at day 1 with Marek's vaccine if available. At 2 weeks, give Newcastle (live B1 strain) via eye drop or drinking water. Repeat at 6 weeks with La Sota strain. For layers and breeders, boost every 3 months. Avian Influenza vaccine is not allowed in many African countriesâcheck with your vet. Fowl Pox vaccine is given at 8 weeks by wing web stab. Always use clean equipment: boil syringes for 10 minutes, use one needle per 10 birds. For medications, keep a farm kit: oxytetracycline (broad-spectrum antibiotic), amprolium (for coccidiosis), ivermectin (for parasites), and electrolytes. Dosages: oxytetracycline 20 mg/kg for 5 days in water; amprolium 1 g per 2 litres of water for 5 days; ivermectin 0.2 mg/kg injected under skin. Never use antibiotics without vet adviceâresistance and residues harm your business. Store vaccines at 2-8Â°C in a fridge, not freezer. Protect from sunlight. Record every vaccination: date, vaccine name, batch number, and bird age. In remote areas, organise a vaccine day with neighbours to share costs. A well-vaccinated flock grows faster and lays more eggs. Budget about $0.10 per bird per vaccine dose. That's small compared to losing your whole flock.

lessons.title: Parasite Control: Internal and External
lessons.body: Ostriches suffer from both internal and external parasites, especially in warm, humid African climates. Internal parasites include roundworms (Ascaridia), tapeworms, and coccidia. Signs: poor growth, dull feathers, diarrhoea, and worms in droppings. Deworm every 3 months with fenbendazole (10 mg/kg orally) or ivermectin (0.2 mg/kg under skin). For coccidia, use amprolium (1 g per 2 L water for 5 days) or sulfa drugs. Rotate pastures to break the life cycleârest each paddock for 30 days. Keep feed and water off the ground. External parasites are ticks, mites, lice, and fleas. Ticks transmit diseases like avian spirochaetosis. Check under wings, around the vent, and on the neck weekly. Treat with permethrin spray (0.5% solution) or dust with diatomaceous earth. For severe infestations, use ivermectin injection (0.2 mg/kg) every 2 weeks for 3 treatments. Mites cause feather loss and anaemia. Clean and spray houses with 2% caustic soda or commercial acaricide. In Africa, tick control is criticalâuse tick grease on ears and around the vent. Keep grass short around pens. Introduce guinea fowl or chickens? Noâthey carry diseases. Instead, use rotational grazing with cattle? No, ostriches are separate. Quarantine new birds and treat them for parasites before mixing. Record all treatments: date, drug, dose, and withdrawal period (meat: 14 days for ivermectin; eggs: 7 days). Never underdoseâit creates resistant parasites. A parasite-free flock gains 20% more weight.

lessons.title: Recognizing Signs of Illness and Injury
lessons.body: Ostriches hide illness until they are very sickâa survival instinct. You must observe your flock daily, ideally at dawn and dusk. Healthy ostriches are alert, eat well, and move actively. Sick ones separate from the group, stand hunched, or lie down often. Key signs: drooping wings, closed eyes, pale comb/wattles, and laboured breathing. Check droppings: normal is firm, dark green with white urate. Watery, bloody, or yellow droppings mean trouble. Injuries are common from fighting, fences, or predators. Look for limping, swollen joints, cuts, or bleeding. A broken leg is obviousâthe bird cannot stand. For wounds, clean with saline or diluted iodine (1:10). Apply antibiotic spray and bandage. For fractures, immobilise with splint and call a vet. Other signs: weight loss (weigh monthly), reduced egg production, soft-shelled eggs, and unusual behaviour like head shaking or circling. Take temperature: normal is 39-40Â°C. Above 41Â°C indicates fever. In Africa, heat stress causes panting, wing spreading, and collapse. Move birds to shade, spray water, and add electrolytes. Keep a notebook: record any abnormality, date, and action. Early isolation of sick birds prevents spread. If more than 3 birds show same signs in 24 hours, call a vet immediately. Remember: a ostrich that is down and cannot rise is an emergencyâit may die within hours. Act fast.

lessons.title: First Aid and Basic Veterinary Procedures
lessons.body: First aid saves lives before the vet arrives. Keep a farm kit: sterile gloves, saline, iodine, antibiotic powder, bandages, scissors, tweezers, syringes (1ml, 5ml, 10ml), needles (18G, 21G), and a thermometer. For bleeding wounds, apply direct pressure with clean cloth for 5 minutes. Clean with saline, apply iodine, then antibiotic powder. Bandage looselyâtoo tight cuts circulation. For broken bones, splint with a stick and vet wrap. Do not try to set a fracture yourself; immobilise and call for help. For heat stress, move bird to shade, pour cool water on legs and neck, and give electrolytes (1 sachet per 5 L water) via crop tube if needed. For poisoning (e.g., from mouldy feed), give activated charcoal (1 g/kg body weight) mixed in water. For bloat (common after eating too much lucerne), pass a stomach tube to release gasâonly if trained. Injections: intramuscular (IM) in breast muscle, subcutaneous (SC) under loose skin on neck. Use 18G needle for IM, 21G for SC. Always aspirate before injecting IMâif blood appears, withdraw and reposition. For oral medications, use a crop tube or syringe without needle at the side of the beak. Restrain birds by placing a hood over the head or holding wings close to body. Never lift an ostrich by the neck. Record all treatments. If you are unsure, do not guessâcall a vet. Basic first aid can reduce mortality by 30% on your farm.

lessons.title: Working with Veterinarians and Diagnostic Labs
lessons.body: A good veterinarian is your partner in ostrich farming. In Africa, find a vet with poultry or ratite experience. Contact your local veterinary office or agricultural extension officer for referrals. Establish a relationship before an emergencyâinvite the vet for a farm visit once a year. Keep a file with your vet's phone number, the nearest diagnostic lab, and a map to your farm. When a disease outbreak occurs, call the vet immediately. Describe symptoms, number of affected birds, and recent changes (feed, weather, new birds). Collect samples for diagnosis: blood (2 ml in EDTA tube), swabs from throat/cloaca, and fresh droppings. For dead birds, submit the whole carcass in a sealed plastic bag on iceânever freeze. Diagnostic labs test for Avian Influenza, Newcastle, Salmonella, and parasites. Results take 2-7 days. While waiting, isolate sick birds and disinfect equipment. In remote areas, use mobile labs or send samples via courier. Costs: basic blood test $10-20, PCR for viruses $30-50. It's worth itâwrong treatment wastes money and kills birds. Work with the vet to create a health plan: vaccination schedule, deworming calendar, and biosecurity rules. Biosecurity: footbaths at entry, limit visitors, and quarantine new birds for 30 days. Keep records of all vet visits, prescriptions, and lab results. Share them with your vet for better advice. A strong vet-farmer relationship reduces losses and builds a sustainable ostrich business.

quiz.q: Which disease is caused by a virus and spreads through wild birds and contaminated water?
quiz.explanation: Avian Influenza is a viral disease spread by wild birds and contaminated water.

quiz.q: What is a common sign of Newcastle disease in ostriches?
quiz.explanation: Newcastle disease attacks the nervous system, causing twisted necks and paralysis.

quiz.q: Which medication is used to treat coccidiosis in ostriches?
quiz.explanation: Amprolium is specifically used to treat coccidiosis.

quiz.q: At what age should chicks receive the first Newcastle vaccine?
quiz.explanation: The first Newcastle vaccine is given at 2 weeks of age.

quiz.q: How should vaccines be stored?
quiz.explanation: Vaccines must be stored at 2-8Â°C in a refrigerator, not frozen.

quiz.q: What is the correct dose of oxytetracycline for ostriches?
quiz.explanation: Oxytetracycline is given at 20 mg/kg body weight for 5 days.

quiz.q: Which internal parasite is treated with fenbendazole?
quiz.explanation: Fenbendazole is effective against roundworms and other internal parasites.

quiz.q: How often should you deworm ostriches in warm, humid climates?
quiz.explanation: Deworming every 3 months is recommended in warm, humid African climates.

quiz.q: What is a sign of external parasite infestation?
quiz.explanation: External parasites like mites cause feather loss and anaemia.

quiz.q: Which chemical is used to treat external parasites?
quiz.explanation: Permethrin spray is used to control ticks, mites, and lice.

quiz.q: What is the normal body temperature of an ostrich?
quiz.explanation: Normal ostrich body temperature is 39-40Â°C.

quiz.q: Which sign indicates a sick ostrich?
options: B) Drooping wings and closed eyes
quiz.explanation: Drooping wings and closed eyes are clear signs of illness.

quiz.q: What should you do first for a bleeding wound?
quiz.explanation: Direct pressure with a clean cloth stops bleeding initially.

quiz.q: How do you treat a broken leg in an ostrich?
options: B) Immobilise with a splint and call a vet
quiz.explanation: Immobilise the fracture with a splint and seek veterinary help.

quiz.q: What is the correct route for intramuscular injection in ostriches?
quiz.explanation: Intramuscular injections are given in the breast muscle.

quiz.q: What should you do before injecting intramuscularly?
options: A) Aspirate to check for blood
quiz.explanation: Aspirating ensures the needle is not in a blood vessel.

quiz.q: Which sample is best for diagnosing viral diseases?
quiz.explanation: Blood in EDTA tube is used for PCR and serology tests.

quiz.q: How should a dead bird be submitted to a diagnostic lab?
options: B) On ice, sealed in plastic
quiz.explanation: Submit the carcass on ice, sealed, never frozen.

quiz.q: What is a key biosecurity measure on an ostrich farm?
quiz.explanation: Footbaths at entry reduce the spread of pathogens.

quiz.q: How long should new birds be quarantined?
quiz.explanation: A 30-day quarantine helps prevent disease introduction.

quiz.q: Which vaccine is given by wing web stab?
quiz.explanation: Fowl Pox vaccine is administered by wing web stab.

quiz.q: What is the withdrawal period for ivermectin in meat?
quiz.explanation: Ivermectin has a 14-day withdrawal period for meat.

quiz.q: Which condition causes bloat in ostriches?
quiz.explanation: Overeating lucerne or other rich feed can cause bloat.

quiz.q: What is the first aid for heat stress?
options: A) Move to shade and apply cool water
quiz.explanation: Cooling the bird and providing shade are immediate actions.

quiz.q: Which drug is used to treat coccidiosis?
quiz.explanation: Amprolium is the drug of choice for coccidiosis.

quiz.q: What is the recommended concentration of chlorine in drinking water for ostriches?
quiz.explanation: 2-3 ppm chlorine helps disinfect water without harming birds.

quiz.q: Which parasite is controlled by rotating pastures?
quiz.explanation: Rotating pastures breaks the life cycle of internal worms.

quiz.q: What is a common sign of Avian Influenza?
options: A) Sudden death and swollen head
quiz.explanation: Avian Influenza causes sudden death and swollen heads.

quiz.q: How often should you check for external parasites?
quiz.explanation: Weekly checks under wings and around the vent are recommended.

quiz.q: What is the role of a veterinarian in ostrich farming?
options: B) Create health plans and diagnose diseases
quiz.explanation: Vets help with vaccination schedules, biosecurity, and diagnosis.
